idea: Train a domain classifier and select the most target-like documents. Steps: (1) Exact-dedupe the pool (hash of whitespace-normalised text; also drop near-duplicates sharing the same first 200 chars). (2) Fit TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(1,4), sublinear_tf=True, max_features=200k, lowercase=False) on the first 3000 chars of each doc; train LogisticRegression (C=1, class_weight='balanced') with positives = 200 target_sample docs and negatives = a seeded random 4000 pool docs; score all pool docs. (3) Self-training round: retrain with positives = target_sample + top 1500 scored pool docs, negatives = bottom 6000 scored docs; rescore. (4) Add a cheap heuristic bonus for WikiText formatting (doc starts with '= ' and contains ' @-@ ' or ' , ' / ' . ' spaced punctuation) and a penalty for junk (low fraction of common-English-word tokens, e.g. scrambled-letter docs, code, coupon spam). (5) Sort by score descending, count tokens with tiktoken gpt2 (or estimate len/4 if time is tight), keep top docs until ~T tokens are reached (if the clearly-target-like set, score > 0.5, has fewer than T tokens, keep just that set plus the next best docs up to at least 0.6T and let it cycle). (6) Shuffle the selected indices with the CURATE_SEED-seeded RNG and return.
why: The target is WikiText-style Wikipedia articles while the pool is half off-domain/junk/duplicated, so spending the fixed T-token budget only on deduplicated target-like documents should cut bpb far more than a random half of the pool.
outcome: dev 1.9334 against 1.9399 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Add a whole-document damage filter on top of the current pipeline; dedupe, classifier, self-training and final shuffle stay as they are. The classifier only sees char n-grams of the first 3000 chars, so it cannot catch word-shuffled, mid-document-corrupted or internally repetitive wiki-looking docs.

(a) Reference bigram set: build a set of lowercase word bigrams (whitespace split) from the 200 target_sample docs plus the 1500 highest-scored pool docs.

(b) Bigram coverage per candidate: for each pool doc with classifier score > 0.3, take three 1500-char windows (head, middle, tail). For each window compute the fraction of its word bigrams found in the reference set; for the pool docs that contributed to the set, subtract their own contribution by requiring a bigram count of at least 2 across reference docs. Keep the minimum over the three windows as cov_min.

(c) Repetition per candidate: compute zlib compression ratio len(zlib.compress(doc)) / len(doc) on the full doc.

(d) Calibrate on target_sample: compute the same two statistics for the target docs using leave-one-out bigram counts. Set cov_thr = the 2nd percentile of target cov_min minus 0.03, and zr_lo / zr_hi = the 1st / 99th percentile of target compression ratio, widened by 0.03 each side.

(e) Apply: subtract 1.0 from the final score (effectively dropping the doc) if cov_min < cov_thr or the compression ratio falls outside [zr_lo, zr_hi]. Then select top docs up to ~T tokens as before. If the surviving set with score > 0.5 holds fewer than T tokens, let it cycle rather than back-filling with damaged docs.
why: The pool appears to contain wiki-formatted docs that are damaged (shuffled, corrupted or repetitive) beyond the first 3000 chars, which the prefix classifier cannot see, and removing them should leave cleaner in-domain tokens for the fixed 300-step budget.
outcome: dev 1.9105 against 1.9334 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Strengthen the damage filter (step 4b) in two ways; leave dedupe, classifier, self-training, selection and shuffle unchanged.

(1) Purify the reference with a second pass. After the current first pass marks damaged docs, rebuild the bigram document-count table from target_sample plus the top 3000 scored pool docs that were NOT flagged in pass 1. Then build one set, ref2 = bigrams with document count >= 2, and use it for every candidate, contributor or not. This replaces the current rule where non-contributors are checked against the raw count table, which accepts any bigram seen once, including bigrams from shuffled docs that got into the reference.

(2) Scan the whole document instead of only head, middle and tail. For each candidate with score > 0.3, split the full lowercase word list into consecutive non-overlapping chunks of 250 words (merge a tail shorter than 80 words into the previous chunk). Compute the bigram coverage of each chunk against ref2. Keep two statistics per doc: cov_min (minimum over chunks) and cov_mean (mean over chunks).

Calibrate both on target_sample with the same procedure; the count >= 2 rule gives leave-one-out for targets. Set thr_min = 3rd percentile of target cov_min minus 0.02, and thr_mean = 3rd percentile of target cov_mean minus 0.01. Flag a doc as damaged if cov_min < thr_min, or cov_mean < thr_mean, or the zlib ratio is outside the existing band.

For reference docs in pass 2, use the full text up to 40000 chars. Keep the time guards: if time passes t_start + 138 s, fall back to the pass-1 flags. Damaged docs are never selected and the survivors are cycled as now.
why: The reference bigram set is currently contaminated by high-scoring shuffled docs and only three windows are checked, so word-shuffled or partly corrupted wiki-looking docs probably still get through and waste training tokens.
outcome: dev 1.9106 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Make deduplication quality-aware and stop back-filling with low-scored docs. Classifier, self-training, heuristics, damage filter and shuffle stay unchanged.

(1) In step 1, keep only the exact dedupe (hash of whitespace-normalised full text). Remove the 'same first 200 chars' drop, so every distinct variant of an article gets scored and damage-checked.

(2) After the damage filter, group the surviving docs by near-duplicate key and keep one representative per group. Use two keys and merge groups with union-find: (a) the first 200 chars of the whitespace-normalised text, for docs of at least 200 chars; (b) the title line, for docs whose first line matches '^= [^=].* =$', using that line lowercased. Within each group choose the representative in this order: not damaged, then classifier score > 0.5, then longest text, then highest final score. Mark every other member as dropped, treated like damaged and never selected. This stops a truncated or corrupted copy that happens to come first in the pool from displacing the clean full copy, and stops several variants of one article from all being selected.

(3) In step 5, remove the min_tokens = 0.6*T back-fill. Stop selecting as soon as final <= 0.5 or T*1.01 tokens are reached, and let the trainer cycle a shorter list. Keep a safety floor: only if the selected set holds fewer than 0.1*T tokens, continue down the ranking to 0.1*T.

Keep all time guards. If the classifier prefix calibration has to shrink because more docs are now vectorised, that is acceptable.
why: The current head-200 dedupe keeps whichever copy appears first, so a damaged or truncated copy can displace the clean one, and the 0.6T back-fill can admit spam that the damage filter never checks because it only looks at docs scoring above 0.3.
outcome: dev 1.9221 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

why: If the clean in-domain set is smaller than T, fresh clean English seen early should teach more than repeating the same articles, and ending on pure in-domain text keeps the final steps on target; experiment 4 got worse when back-filling was removed, though it changed dedupe at the same time so that evidence is only suggestive.
outcome: dev 1.9208 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Build the full T-token training order explicitly so the trainer never cycles the mixed list: low-scored back-fill docs are seen once, early, and the rest of the budget is in-domain repeats. Dedupe, classifier, self-training, heuristics and damage filter stay unchanged.

(1) Split the current selection in two. core = selected undamaged docs with final > 0.5, in score order, capped at T*1.01 tokens. backfill = the docs the existing min_tokens = 0.6*T rule adds after the core (final <= 0.5, undamaged), exactly as chosen now. Keep per-doc token counts from the existing tiktoken / char-ratio counting.

(2) If the core alone holds >= T tokens, or the backfill is empty, return the seeded-shuffled selection exactly as now.

(3) Otherwise build the order explicitly:
- Pass 1: core + backfill, seeded shuffle together (this is the current list, about 0.6*T tokens).
- Pass 2, 3, ...: core only, with a fresh seeded shuffle each pass, appended until the running total reaches T*1.01 tokens. The last pass may be cut short.
Return the concatenation. Indices repeat, which is allowed.

(4) Safety: if the core holds fewer than 0.05*T tokens, fall back to the current behaviour. Keep all time guards; the extra work is list operations only.
why: Experiments 4 and 5 suggest the clean in-domain core is well under T and that both no back-fill and a full off-domain back-fill hurt, so showing the back-fill once early and spending the cycled 40% of the budget on in-domain text alone should improve the mix and make the final steps purely in-domain.
outcome: dev 1.9067 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Re-apply the explicit T-token order from experiment 6 (it scored 1.9067, the lowest so far) and add a quality gate on the back-fill docs. Dedupe, classifier, self-training, heuristics and the core damage filter stay unchanged.

(1) Core = undamaged docs with final > 0.5, in score order, capped at T*1.01 tokens. If the core alone holds >= T tokens, return it shuffled exactly as now.

(2) Back-fill candidates = remaining docs in descending final order, added until core + back-fill reaches 0.6*T tokens, as now. Each candidate must first pass a lazy clean-text check. This check also runs for docs with classifier score <= 0.3, which the current damage filter never examines. Keep `cnt`, `ref2`, `cov_thr`, `zr_lo` and `zr_hi` alive for it. A candidate passes if:
- it is not flagged as damaged;
- its full-doc zlib ratio is inside [zr_lo - 0.03, zr_hi + 0.06];
- its _cov_min against the raw bigram count table `cnt` is >= 0.6 * cov_thr, which rejects word-shuffled and letter-scrambled text;
- _common_frac of its first 3000 chars is >= 0.8 * the 5th percentile of the target values;
- _alpha_frac of its first 1000 chars is >= af_thr.
Skip docs that fail and continue down the ranking. Stop at 0.6*T tokens or at t_start + 158 s. If the damage-filter statistics are unavailable, use only the common_frac and alpha_frac tests.

(3) Build the order:
- Pass 1: core + accepted back-fill, seeded shuffle together.
- Pass 2, 3, ...: core only, with a fresh seeded shuffle each pass, appended until the running total reaches T*1.01 tokens. Use the per-doc token counts already computed.
The trainer then never cycles the mixed list: back-fill is seen once, early, and the rest of the budget is in-domain.

(4) Safety: if the core holds fewer than 0.05*T tokens, fall back to the current behaviour. Keep all time guards.
why: Experiment 6's order gave the lowest dev bpb so far, and the back-fill it uses is currently taken by classifier rank alone without any damage check below score 0.3, so gating it should remove shuffled or spam text from the one pass where off-domain docs appear.
outcome: dev 1.8993 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Build on the explicit T-token order with gated back-fill from experiment 7 (the lowest dev so far, 1.8993), and change where the back-fill sits: front-load it so the last part of training is purely in-domain. Dedupe, classifier, self-training, heuristics and the damage filter stay unchanged.

(1) Core = undamaged docs with final > 0.5, in score order, capped at T*1.01 tokens, with per-doc token counts from the existing tiktoken / char-ratio counting. If the core alone holds >= T tokens, return it shuffled exactly as now.

(2) Back-fill = remaining docs in descending final order, added until core + back-fill reaches 0.6*T tokens. Each candidate must pass the lazy clean-text check of experiment 7, which also runs for docs with classifier score <= 0.3. Keep `cnt`, `cov_thr`, `zr_lo` and `zr_hi` alive for it. A candidate passes if:
- it is not flagged as damaged;
- its full-doc zlib ratio is inside [zr_lo - 0.03, zr_hi + 0.06];
- its _cov_min against the raw count table `cnt` is >= 0.6 * cov_thr;
- _common_frac of its first 3000 chars is >= 0.8 * the 5th percentile of the target values;
- _alpha_frac of its first 1000 chars is >= af_thr.
Skip docs that fail and continue down the ranking. Stop at 0.6*T tokens or at t_start + 158 s. If the damage-filter statistics are unavailable, use only the common_frac and alpha_frac tests.

(3) Build the order (this is the new part):
- Seeded-shuffle the core and split it into two halves, H1 and H2, by token count.
- Segment A: all back-fill docs + H1, seeded shuffle together.
- Segment B: H2, shuffled.
- Segments C, D, ...: the full core with a fresh seeded shuffle each pass, appended until the running total reaches T*1.01 tokens. The last pass may be cut short.
Return A + B + C + ... The trainer then never cycles. Every back-fill doc is seen once, inside the earliest part of the stream (about the first 0.6*T - core/2 tokens), still mixed with in-domain text. Everything after that is in-domain only.

(4) Safety: if the core holds fewer than 0.05*T tokens, or no back-fill doc is accepted, fall back to the current behaviour (shuffled selection, cycled). Keep all time guards.
why: Gated back-fill seen once plus core-only repeats gave the lowest dev so far, and moving the off-domain text into the earliest high-learning-rate steps should leave a longer purely in-domain stretch for the model to settle on the target distribution.
outcome: dev 1.9118 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

why: Experiment 7's explicit non-cycling order with quality-gated back-fill gave the lowest dev bpb (1.8993), so a time-safer variant that spreads the back-fill evenly and ends on pure in-domain text should keep that gain, assuming the rejection was caused by time or noise.
outcome: dev 1.9022 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

why: Gated back-fill seen once plus in-domain repeats gave the lowest dev so far (1.8993), while filling up to T with off-domain prose was worse (1.9208), so a smaller off-domain share may lower bpb further.
outcome: dev 1.9012 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

why: In experiments 6 and 7 the gate alone moved dev bpb from 1.9067 to 1.8993 by keeping shuffled, spam and junk text out of the 0.6*T back-fill, and applying it without repeated indices or late work tests that gain while avoiding the features common to every rejected low-bpb run, although the real cause of those rejections is unknown to me.
outcome: dev 1.9027 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected

why: Gated back-fill seen once plus in-domain repeats gave the lowest dev bpb (1.8993), and halving the back-fill was slightly worse, so more clean unique text in place of one more core repeat may help; I still do not know why experiments 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 were rejected despite lower dev bpb, so this may be rejected for the same unknown reason.
outcome: dev 1.9052 against 1.9105 for the best at the time, rejected
